title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence II
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

A good subsequence is built from matched pairs, outside in: the outer pair, then the next pair inside, and so on, ending with the equal middle pair. The "no equal neighbours" rule then says only this: **each pair's letter differs from the letter of the pair just inside it**. Even length is automatic when we only ever add pairs.

Plain longest-palindromic-subsequence DP works on intervals `s[i..j]`. Here we must also know the letter of the outermost pair, because a new pair of letter `c` may only wrap an inside whose outer letter is not `c`. So the state is (interval, outer letter). Trying every subsequence instead would cost O(2^n).

## Approach

1. Let `dp[j][c]` be the longest good subsequence of `s[i..j]` whose outer letter is `c` (0 if none), and `prev` the same table for `i + 1`. Fill `i` from right to left, `j` from left to right.
2. Skipping an end is always allowed: `dp[j][c] = max(prev[j][c], dp[j - 1][c])`.
3. If `s[i] === s[j]`, they can be the outer pair: take `inside`, the best of `prev[j - 1][c]` over letters `c` other than `s[i]` (0 means an empty inside, giving the middle pair), and offer `inside + 2` for letter `s[i]`.
4. After `i = 0`, the answer is the largest entry of `prev[n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "bbabab"` (indexes 0 to 5).

- `i = 2, j = 4`: both are `a`. The inside `s[3..3] = "b"` holds no good subsequence, so `inside = 0` and `dp[4][a] = 2` ("aa").
- `i = 1, j = 5`: both are `b`. Inside `s[2..4]` the best with an outer letter other than `b` is 2 (letter `a`), so `dp[5][b] = 4` ("baab").
- Nothing longer exists: the only subsequence of length 6 is the whole string, which is not a palindrome. The largest entry of the final row is `4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(26 · n²): every interval looks at all 26 letters a constant number of times.
- Space: O(26 · n): only the rows for `i` and `i + 1` are kept.

## Pitfalls

- Keeping just one (length, letter) per interval fails on ties: the inside may reach the same length with outer letter `c` or `d`, and only the `d` one can be wrapped by a `c` pair.
- An empty inside is fine: the two wrapped letters become the middle pair, the one place where equal neighbours are allowed.
- Do not count a single middle character as in the classic problem: odd lengths are not good.
- The answer can be `0`, for example when all letters are different.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `letter` | `s` converted to letter indexes 0 to 25 |
| `prev` | the table for start `i + 1` (for intervals `s[i + 1..j]`) |
| `dp[j][c]` | longest good subsequence of `s[i..j]` whose outer letter is `c` |
| `i`, `j` | start and end of the interval |
| `inside` | best inner length that a pair `s[i]`, `s[j]` may wrap |

narration.3: Turn the letters into indexes 0 to 25 so they can address the letter dimension.
narration.4: Row for start n: every interval there is empty, so every entry is 0.
narration.5: Fill interval starts from right to left, so row i + 1 is ready when row i needs it.
narration.6: dp[j][c] will be the longest good subsequence of s[i..j] whose outer letter is c.
narration.7: Grow the interval's end to the right.
narration.9: Skip s[i] (row i + 1) or skip s[j] (same row, one shorter): either keeps the outer letter.
narration.11: Equal ends can be the outer pair of a good subsequence.
narration.12: inside is the best inner part this pair may wrap; 0 means they become the middle pair.
narration.14: The inner part's outer letter must differ from the new pair's letter.
narration.18: Wrap the inside with the pair and keep it if it is longer.
narration.21: Row i is complete; it becomes the previous row for start i - 1.
narration.23: The answer for the whole string is the best over all outer letters.
